This stress value is similar to the peak von Mises stress found for the 39.6 m-diameter tank floor in the previous report [4], which demonstrates that the maximum residual stresses, which are developed on the floor welds, are independent of floor diameter. The residual stresses of the tank floor strongly depend on the heat input, constraint design, and weld pass length. The highest residual stresses were observed in highly constrained point locations and interactions of plate edges. - Under similar constraint conditions, the maximum normal displacement increases with increasing tank diameter, rising from 114.5 mm in the 24 m diameter floor to 130.8 mm in the 39.6 m diameter tank floor. With less constraint on the outer edges of the floor, the 32 m diameter tank floor exhibits a greater maximum displacement of 158.5 mm. For distortion control in welding, both diameter size and the weld plate layout or constraint design play significant roles. Introducing more constraints can effectively disrupt the distortion pattern and reduce the extent of distortion. In general, tanks with large diameters and thin floors may potentially experience buckling instability with severe distortions. - Preliminary results from preheating analysis show that the initial residual stress relaxes during the first days and then increases once the salt starts entering the tank. As expected, stresses during preheating are larger in the tank floor when compared to the wall due to the higher constraints of the tank floor, which makes it a critical component suitable for improvement to reduce susceptibility to tank failures. Finally, solving failures in molten salt Thermal Energy Storage (TES) tanks is fundamental for CSP, nuclear, industrial thermal process, and thermal-electrical energy storage technologies. In addition to the recommendations provided in the previous report [4], some recommendations for future work to advance toward a solution to molten salt tank failures include: 1) tank size analysis focused on the relationship between tank diameter and floor thickness, considering initial stress and distortion in the tank floor after welding fabrication; 2) preheating optimization to reduce residual stress while avoiding 35 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. excessive floor distortion; and 3) improving welding process specifications and tank welding fabrication strategies to reduce residual stress while controlling distortion in the tank floor. 4.2 Products Project Report J.D.
